rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its strongest line, "without a number this stays a claim, not a proven contrarian story," is exactly the discipline a founder needs before walking into a reporter's inbox. B has useful shapes, but "Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" turns one distribution fact into a whole market thesis it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" leans on the blog origin as color, but does not prove why that origin matters to the fragrance story.
"Glossier more than doubles its Sephora footprint to 1,400 doors" treats 1,400 as meaningful before proving whether that is large or ordinary inside Sephora's prestige universe.

"the wave of beauty brands extending into scent" is plausible trade framing, but it is not in the update; A correctly asks for trend context, but the kept angle still needs that support before pitching.
A misses a consumer-access angle around Sephora at Kohl's shoppers. It keeps the work mostly trade-facing, which is disciplined but leaves one viable reader-protagonist unused.
gaps_in_B: "Glossier, built on saying no to stores" overstates the update. The facts say Glossier was DTC-only for a decade; they do not say the brand built its identity on rejecting stores.

"Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" is a thesis wearing a borrowed coat. One inclusion in Sephora at Kohl's does not prove a test case without performance data or comparable brands.
"mid-market and suburban shoppers" and "coastal-urban" invent audience geography. The update says US, Canada, and Sephora at Kohl's; it does not map the shoppers.

"scent, unlike skincare or makeup, is a category that historically underperforms in pure DTC" may be true, but it is not supplied here. B flags the causal link as an inference, then smuggles in the category premise anyway.
